title: Air Navigation Systems Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of navigation aids, GPS, ILS, and Performance-Based Navigation from AIM Chapter 1

questions.question: What is the frequency range for NDB (Nondirectional Beacon) transmitters?
questions.explanation: NDBs operate in the low/medium frequency band of 190 to 535 kHz. According to ICAO Annex 10, the range extends up to 1750 kHz.

questions.question: Why should pilots continuously monitor NDB identification?
options: Because ADF receivers have no flag to warn of erroneous bearing information
Because NDBs transmit variable identification signals
questions.explanation: ADF receivers do not have a 'flag' to warn pilots when erroneous bearing information is being displayed. Noisy identification usually occurs when the ADF needle is erratic.

questions.question: What is the frequency range for VOR stations?
questions.explanation: VORs operate within the 108.0 to 117.95 MHz frequency band (VHF). They are subject to line-of-sight restrictions.

questions.question: When using a VOT (VOR Test Facility) to check VOR accuracy, what should the CDI and OBS show?
options: OBS 0° with FROM indication, or 180° with TO indication
questions.explanation: With the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with 'FROM' indication, or 180° with 'TO' indication. This verifies proper VOR receiver operation.

questions.question: What is the maximum allowable VOR receiver error for IFR flight using a VOT check?
questions.explanation: Under 14 CFR 91.171, the maximum allowable VOR receiver error using a VOT is ±4 degrees. Other methods have different tolerances.

questions.question: What three services does a VORTAC provide?
options: VOR azimuth, TACAN azimuth, and TACAN distance (DME)
NDB bearing, VOR azimuth, and DME
GPS position, VOR azimuth, and altitude
questions.explanation: a VORTAC provides VOR azimuth (for civilian aircraft), TACAN azimuth (for military aircraft), and TACAN distance (DME) from a single collocated site.

questions.question: DME provides what type of distance measurement?
questions.explanation: DME provides slant range distance, not actual horizontal distance. The difference is most noticeable when close to the station at high altitude.

questions.question: What is the operating frequency range of DME?
questions.explanation: DME operates in the UHF band from 960 MHz to 1215 MHz according to ICAO Annex 10.

questions.question: What are the three basic functional parts of an ILS?
questions.explanation: The ILS consists of: guidance information (localizer, glideslope), range information (marker beacons, DME), and visual information (approach lights, runway lights).

questions.question: What is the localizer course width at the runway threshold?
questions.explanation: The localizer is adjusted for a course width of 700 feet at the runway threshold (full scale fly-left to full scale fly-right).

questions.question: What color light and tone code does the ILS Outer Marker (OM) produce?
options: Amber light, alternating dots and dashes
Green light, alternating short and long dashes
questions.explanation: The Outer Marker produces a blue light with continuous dashes (low tone). The Middle Marker is amber with alternating dots/dashes, Inner Marker is white with dots.

questions.question: When flying inbound on an ILS back course without reverse sensing capability, how should course corrections be made?
options: Fly opposite to the needle deflection
questions.explanation: Unless the ILS equipment includes reverse sensing capability, when flying inbound on the back course, steer opposite the needle deflection when making corrections.

questions.question: How does a Simplified Directional Facility (SDF) differ from an ILS localizer?
options: SDF course may not be aligned with runway and may be wider (6° or 12°)
questions.explanation: The SDF course may not be aligned with the runway, and the signal is fixed at either 6° or 12° (vs ILS localizer which is ~5°), resulting in less precision.

questions.question: What happens to NAVAID identification during maintenance?
options: It is removed or may transmit T-E-S-T code
It changes to a different frequency
questions.explanation: During maintenance, coded identification is removed as a warning that the facility is officially off the air. VHF ranges may radiate a T-E-S-T code.

questions.question: What information does an IRU (Inertial Reference Unit) provide?
questions.explanation: IRUs provide aircraft attitude (pitch, roll, heading), position, and velocity using gyros and accelerometers. Position accuracy degrades over time (drift).

questions.question: How many GPS satellites are in the constellation, and how many are needed for 3D position?
questions.explanation: The GPS constellation consists of 24 satellites. A minimum of 4 satellites is necessary for receivers to establish an accurate 3D position.

questions.question: What is RAIM and why is it important?
options: Radio Altitude Indication Method - provides terrain clearance
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring - provides GPS integrity without ground augmentation
Runway Alignment Indicator Mode - aligns with runway
Required Area Information Management - manages flight plans
questions.explanation: RAIM is Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring. It allows the GPS receiver to verify integrity of satellite signals. Without RAIM, there's no assurance of position accuracy.

questions.question: How many satellites does RAIM require for fault detection?
questions.explanation: RAIM requires a minimum of 5 satellites, or 4 satellites with barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly.

questions.question: What is WAAS and what does it improve?
options: Weather Avoidance Alert System - improves weather detection
Wide Area Augmentation System - improves GPS accuracy, integrity, and availability
Warning and Advisory Alert System - improves traffic alerts
Wing Attitude Adjustment System - improves aircraft control
questions.explanation: WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) improves GPS accuracy, integrity, and availability. It enables approaches with vertical guidance (LPV approaches).

questions.question: What frequency does WAAS broadcast on?
questions.explanation: WAAS broadcasts correction messages on the same frequency as GPS (L1, 1575.42 MHz) to WAAS receivers within the coverage area.

questions.question: What is GBAS/GLS?
options: Global Broadcast Alert System / Ground Landing System
Ground Based Augmentation System / GBAS Landing System
GPS Backup Alert System / Glide Landing System
General Broadcast Aviation Service / GPS Localizer System
questions.explanation: GBAS (Ground Based Augmentation System) provides localized differential GPS augmentation. GLS (GBAS Landing System) enables precision approaches similar to ILS.

questions.question: What is the key difference between RNAV and RNP navigation specifications?
options: RNAV uses GPS, RNP uses VOR
RNP includes onboard performance monitoring and alerting (OBPMA)
RNAV is for enroute, RNP is for approaches only
questions.explanation: RNP includes onboard performance monitoring and alerting capability (OBPMA). This allows the aircraft to verify it's meeting navigation performance requirements.

questions.question: What does the numerical designation in 'RNP 1' or 'RNAV 2' represent?
options: The version number of the specification
The lateral navigation accuracy in nautical miles (95% of the time)
questions.explanation: The numerical designation refers to the lateral navigation accuracy in nautical miles that must be achieved at least 95% of the flight time.

questions.question: Can a suitable RNAV system be used as a substitute when a VOR is out of service?
options: No, only ground-based navaids can be used
Yes, a suitable RNAV system can substitute for out-of-service navaids
questions.explanation: A suitable RNAV system can be used as a substitute means of navigation when a VOR, DME, NDB, or other navaid is out of service.

questions.question: What are potential effects of GPS jamming or spoofing?
options: Loss of GPS navigation, unreliable TAWS triggers, erroneous ADS-B outputs, and more
GPS receivers are immune to jamming
questions.explanation: GPS jamming/spoofing can cause loss of navigation, unreliable TAWS warnings, inaccurate position on displays, erroneous ADS-B, and many other system failures.

questions.question: What should pilots do when encountering GPS navigation errors?
options: Continue using GPS and report after landing
Transition to another navigation source and request amended clearances as necessary
questions.explanation: Pilots encountering navigation error events should transition to another source of navigation and request amended clearances from ATC as necessary.

questions.question: VOR accuracy is generally plus or minus how many degrees?
questions.explanation: The accuracy of course alignment of the VOR is excellent, being generally plus or minus 1 degree.

questions.question: What does 'VORW' indicate in a VOR's class designator?
questions.explanation: The letter 'W' (Without voice) indicates VORs without voice transmission capability. Most VORs are equipped for voice transmission on the VOR frequency.

questions.question: What is the VOR Minimum Operational Network (MON)?
options: A network of high-powered VORs for oceanic navigation
A subset of VORs retained as backup when GPS is unavailable
A monitoring system for VOR accuracy
The minimum number of VORs required per state
questions.explanation: As the FAA removes selected VORs from service due to GPS/RNAV adoption, the MON is a subset of VORs retained to provide backup navigation if GPS becomes unavailable.

questions.question: What condition might cause heading errors in aircraft with slaved compass systems during taxi?
options: Magnetic flux fields from materials under taxiways/ramps
questions.explanation: Aircraft with slaved compass systems may experience heading errors caused by magnetic flux fields from materials on the surface or buried under taxiways and ramps.
